## Bisectors
Much of mastering geometry is mastering triangles. This chapter defines points, lines, and circles that all triangles have, and explores their properties.
We start with 2 helpful results to that end. A <i>cevian</i> of a triangle is a line segment from any vertex to the opposite edge.

::: {#lem-7.1.equidis}

Given $\overline{AB}$ and its perpendicular bisector line k, a point is on line k if and only if it is equidistant from A and B.
In other words, line k is exactly the set of points equidistant from A and B.

:::

::: {.proof}

The midpoint $M$ of $\overline{AB}$ is both on line k and equidistant from A and B. Assume C is another point.
"$\to$" If C is on line k, then $\triangle AMC \cong \triangle BMC$ by SAS congruence, so $AC=BC$.
"$\leftarrow$" If $AC=BC$, then $\triangle AMC \cong \triangle BMC$ by SSS congruence, so $m \angle AMC=m \angle BMC=90^\circ$, ie $\overline{CM}\perp \overline{AB}$.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img=np.ones((500,500,3),dtype=np.uint8)*255
a=(100,250)
b=(400,250)
c=(250,100)
m=(250,250)
cv2.line(img,a,b,color,thickness=2)
double_arrow_line(img,(250,50),(250,450), color)
draw_path(img,a,c,b,thickness=1)
add_tick(img,a,m)
add_tick(img,b,m)
draw_path(img,(230,250),(230,230),(250,230), thickness=1) #perp marker
cv2.putText(img,'A',(a[0]-20,a[1]),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'B',(b[0]+10,b[1]),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'C',(c[0]+10,c[1]),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'M',(m[0]+10,m[1]-10),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'k',(260,400),font,0.6,color,2)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

::: {#lem-7.1.angle.bisect}

$\overrightarrow{BD}$ is the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ if and only if D is equidistant from $\overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}$.
In other words, an angle bisector is exactly the set of points equidistant from the 2 rays that form the angle.

:::

::: {.proof}

Let E,F be on $\overrightarrow{BA}, \overrightarrow{BC}$ such that $\overline{DE}\perp \overrightarrow{BA}$ and $\overline{DF}\perp \overrightarrow{BC}$.
Then $DE, DF$ are the distances from D to $\overrightarrow{BA}, \overrightarrow{BC}$ by @lem-6.dist.
"$\to$" If $m \angle ABD=m \angle CBD$, then $\triangle BDE \cong \triangle BDF$ by AAS congruence @lem-3.aas, so $DE=DF$.
"$\leftarrow$" If $DE=DF$, then $\triangle BDE \cong \triangle BDF$ by HL congruence @lem-6.hl, so $m \angle ABD=m \angle CBD$. 

:::

## Circumcenter

::: {#lem-7.circumctr}

Given $\triangle ABC$, the perpendicular bisectors of its 3 sides are concurrent at a point called the <i>circumcenter</i> (point O below).
There is a unique circle passing thru A, B, and C. It is centered at the circumcenter. It is called the <i>circumcircle</i>, which <i>circumscribes</i> $\triangle ABC$, and has <i>circumradius</i> $OA$.<br>
In the special case where $\triangle ABC$ is a right triangle, the circumcenter is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

:::

In particular, just as 2 points determine a line, 3 non collinear points determine a circle.

::: {.proof}

Let O be the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$.
Then by @lem-7.1.equidis: $OA=OB$ and $OB=OC$, so $OA=OC$, so O is on the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AC}$, and $\odot O$ with radius $OA=OB=OC$ circumscribes $\triangle ABC$.<br>
Let $\odot Q$ also circumscribe $\triangle ABC$. Then $QA=QB=QC$, so Q is on the perpendicular bisectors of $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{BC}$, and $\overline{AC}$, so $Q=O$, and $\odot Q$ and $\odot O$ have the same radius.<br>
If $\triangle ABC$ is a right triangle, say with $m \angle C=90^\circ$, let $\overline{MO}$ be the perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AC}$, with M and O its intersections with $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{AB}$.
Then $\overline{MO}\parallel \overline{AB}$ by @lem-2.7, and $AM=CM$, so $AO=BO$ by @lem-5.sas.
The perpendicular bisector of $\overline{AB}$ thus passes thru O, so it is the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$.

:::

## Incenter

::: {#lem-7.tangent}

Line k is tangent to $\odot O$ at point P if and only if line k is perpendicular to $\overline{OP}$.

:::

::: {.proof}

Let A be a point besides P on line k.
"$\to$" Consider $\overline{OA}$, let B be the point where it intersects $\odot O$.
Then $OA=OB+BA=OP+BA>OP$, so P is the closest point to O on line k, so line k is perpendicular to $\overline{OP}$ by @lem-6.dist.
"$\leftarrow$" If line k is perpendicular to $\overline{OP}$, then $OA>OP$ by @lem-6.dist, so A is not on line k.
Line k thus intersects $\odot O$ at 1 point (namely, P), ie is tangent to $\odot O$.

:::

```{python}

p=(240,400)

cv2.circle(img,o,radius=160,color=color,thickness=2)
for j,lbl in enumerate('ABPO'):
    p1=globals()[lbl.lower()]
    q=-10 if j%2 else 20
    cv2.putText(img,lbl,(p1[0],p1[1]+q),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'k',(100,390),font,0.6,color,2)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

::: {#lem-7.inctr}

Given $\triangle ABC$, its 3 angle bisectors are concurrent at a point called the <i>incenter</i> (point $I$ below).
There is a unique circle tangent to all 3 of its sides. It is centered at the incenter. It is called the <i>incircle</i>, which is <i>inscribed</i> in $\triangle ABC$, and has <i>inradius</i> $ID$.

:::

::: {.proof}

Let I be the intersection of the angle bisectors of $\angle A$ and $\angle B$.
Let D, E, F be such that $\overline{AB}\perp \overline{ID}$, $\overline{BC}\perp \overline{IE}$, and $\overline{AC}\perp \overline{IF}$.
Then $ID=IF$ and $ID=IE$, so $IE=IF$, and $\overline{IC}$ bisects $\angle C$, all by @lem-7.1.angle.bisect.
Further, $\odot I$ with radius $ID=IE=IF$ is tangent to all 3 sides by @lem-7.tangent.<br>
Conversely, for any circle tangent to all 3 sides, its 3 radii to those 3 sides must each be perpendicular.
The center must thus be equidistant from all 3 sides, so it must be on all 3 angle bisectors, so its center must be $I$, and its radius must be the distance to any of the 3 sides.
This circle is thus $\odot O$.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false

b=(100,400)
c=(500,400)
d=(100,300)
e=(200,400)

```

::: {#lem-7.inr.area}

The area of a triangle is the product of its inradius and semi perimeter. In symbols, $[ABC]=rs$.

:::

::: {.proof}

Given $\triangle ABC$ with incenter $I$ as above, we have $[ABC]=[AIB]+[BIC]+[AIC]$ $=AB \cdot ID/2+ BC \cdot IE/2+AC \cdot IF/2$ $=(AB+BC+AC)\cdot r/2=rs$.

:::

Angle bisectors are useful beyond the incenter and its properties.

::: {#lem-7.abt}

<i>Angle bisector theorem:</i> given $\triangle ABC$ with D on $\overline{BC}$ such that $\overline{AD}$ bisects $\angle BAC$, then $AB/BD=AC/CD$.

:::

::: {.proof}

Draw a line thru B parallel to $\overline{AC}$. Extend $\overline{AD}$ to this line. Let E be the point of intersection.
Then $\triangle ACD \sim \triangle EBD$ by @lem-5.sim.plel2, so $AC/CD=BE/BD$, and $m \angle CAD=m \angle BED$.
So $\triangle ABE$ is isosceles with $AB=BE$ by @lem-3.6.isosc, and $AC/CD=AB/BD$.

:::


## Triangle medians

A <i>median</i> of a triangle is a segment from any vertex to its opposite side's midpoint.

::: {#lem-7.centroid}

A triangle's 3 medians are concurrent at a point called the <i>centroid</i>.
The 3 medians split the triangle into 6 smaller triangles of equal area.
Conversely, any 3 concurrent cevians that split the triangle into 6 smaller triangles of equal area must be medians.
On any median, the centroid is 2/3 of the way from a vertex to the opposite side.

:::

::: {.proof}

Given $\triangle ABC$ with medians $\overline{AD}$ and $\overline{BE}$ that intersect at G, and F on $\overline{AB}$ such that $\overline{CF}$ passes thru G.
For convenience, let $x:=[ABC]/6$. We use @lem-4.3 repeatedly.
Since D is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$, we have $[ABD]=[ACD]$ and $[BDG]=[CDG]$, and so $[ABG]=[ACG]$.
Since E is the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$, we have $[ABE]=[BCE]$ and $[AEG]=[CEG]$, and so $[ABG]=[BCG]$.
Thus, $[ABG]=[ACG]=[BCG]=2x$, and $[BDG]=[CDG]=[CEG]=[AEG]=x$. Next,
$$\frac{AF}{BF}= \frac{[AFG]}{[BFG]}= \frac{[ACF]}{[BCF]}= \frac{[AFG]+2x}{[BFG]+2x}$$
Cross multiplying and using $x>0$, we get $[AFG]=[BFG]$, so $AF=BF$, $\overline{CF}$ is a median, and it is concurrent with the other 2.
We have also shown all 6 small triangles that the medians create have area x.
Conversely, if all we know is that $\overline{AD}$, $\overline{BE}$, and $\overline{CF}$ are cevians, concurrent at G, that split $\triangle ABC$ into 6 smaller triangles of equal area, then $[ABD]=[ACD]$, so $BD=CD$ and $\overline{AD}$ is in fact a median.
Similarly, $\overline{BE}$ and $\overline{CF}$ are medians too.
Finally, from $[ABD]=3x$ and $[BDG]=x$ we get $AD=3DG$, ie the centroid is 2/3 of the way from a vertex to the opposite side.

::: 

```{python}
#| echo: false

a=(230,90)
b=(90,370)
c=(510,370)
d=(300,370)
e=midpt(a,c)
f=midpt(a,b)
g=get_intersection(a,d,b,e)
draw_path(img,a,b,c,a)
for j,lbl in enumerate('ABCDEFG'):
    p1=globals()[lbl.lower()]
    q=20 if j%2 else -10
    cv2.putText(img,lbl,(p1[0],p1[1]+q),font,0.6,color,2)
img1=img.copy()
cv2.line(img,a,d,color,thickness=1)
cv2.line(img,b,e,color,thickness=1)
cv2.line(img,c,f,color,thickness=1)
add_tick(img,b,d)
add_tick(img,c,d)
for q in [-5,5]:
    add_tick(img,a,e,offset_px=q)
    add_tick(img,c,e,offset_px=q)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

::: {#lem-7.medial}

Given $\triangle ABC$ with D, E, F the midpoints of its sides as below. The following are equivalent:

- D, E, F are their respective sides' midpoints.
- $\overline{AB}\parallel \overline{DE}$, $\overline{AC}\parallel \overline{DF}$, and $\overline{BC}\parallel \overline{EF}$.
- $\triangle DEF \cong \triangle AFE \cong \triangle FBD \cong \triangle EDC$.

In which case $\triangle DEF \sim \triangle ABC$ (with ratio 1/2) is called the <i>medial triangle</i>.
Further, $\triangle DEF$ has the same medians (and hence, same centroid) as $\triangle ABC$.

:::

::: {.proof}

1 $\to$ 2 follows from @lem-5.sas. 2 $\to$ 3: from $\overline{AB}\parallel \overline{DE}$, we get $m \angle AFE=m \angle DEF$ by @lem-2.7.
Likewise, from $\overline{AC}\parallel \overline{DF}$, we get $m \angle AEF=m \angle DFE$.
So $\triangle DEF \cong \triangle AFE$ by ASA congruence @lem-3.asa. By symmetric arguments, we also get $\triangle DEF \cong \triangle FBD$ and $\triangle DEF \cong \triangle EDC$.<br>
3 $\to$ 1: CPCTC says that $AF=BF$, $AE=CE$, and $BD=CD$.<br>
Since $\overline{AF}\parallel \overline{ED}$ and $\overline{AE}\parallel \overline{FD}$, we have that $\overline{AD}$ bisects $\overline{EF}$ by @lem-3.pgram.
$\overline{AD}$ is thus a median for $\triangle DEF$, as are $\overline{BE}$ and $\overline{CF}$ by the same argument.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
draw_path(img1,d,e,f,d,thickness=1)
cv2.arrowedLine(img1,(200,370),(210,370),color,tipLength=1.0) #parallel markers
cv2.arrowedLine(img1,(270,230),(280,230),color,tipLength=1.0)
cv2.arrowedLine(img1,(300,160),(307,167),color,tipLength=1.0)
cv2.arrowedLine(img1,(230,300),(237,307),color,tipLength=1.0)
cv2.arrowedLine(img1,(190,170),(195,160),color,tipLength=1.0)
cv2.arrowedLine(img1,(330,310),(335,300),color,tipLength=1.0)
show_geometry_image(img1)
```

$$G= \big( \frac{x_1+x_2+x_3}{3}, \frac{y_1+y_2+y_3}{3}\big)$$

This shows the centroid is the center of mass of a triangle (assuming equal point masses at the vertices).
Finding the centroid is a 2D problem that can be reduced to 2 1D problems.


## Orthocenter

::: {#lem-7.orthoctr}

A triangle's 3 altitudes are concurrent at the <i>orthocenter</i>, which is the circumcenter for the triangle of which the original is the medial triangle.<br>
If $\triangle ABC$ is a right triangle with $m \angle C=90^\circ$, then C is the orthocenter.

:::

::: {.proof}

Given $\triangle ABC$, draw lines thru each vertex parallel to the opposite side.
They will form a larger $\triangle JKL$ as below, of which $\triangle ABC$ is the medial triangle, by construction and @lem-7.medial, which also says that A, B, C are the midpoints of the sides of $\triangle JKL$.
The altitudes for A, B, and C are perpendicular to $\overline{KL}$, $\overline{JL}$, and $\overline{JK}$, respectively by @lem-2.7.
These altitudes are thus perpendicular bisectors of the 3 sides of $\triangle JKL$, which are concurrent by @lem-7.circumctr.<br>
For a right triangle, the 2 legs are also altitudes, and they intersect at the right angle, which must be the orthocenter.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img = np.ones((500,600,3), dtype=np.uint8) * 255
h=(300,300)
l=(230,90)
k=(90,370)
j=(510,370)
c=(300,370)
b=midpt(l,j)
a=midpt(l,k)
draw_path(img,a,b,c,a)
draw_path(img,(300,230),c,k,l,j,c,thickness=1)
for ji,lbl in enumerate('LKJCBAH'):
    p1=globals()[lbl.lower()]
    q=25 if ji%2 else -10
    cv2.putText(img,lbl,(p1[0],p1[1]+q),font,0.6,color,2)
draw_perp(img,a,b,c)
draw_perp(img,b,a,c)
draw_path(img,(320,230),(320,250),(300,250),thickness=1) #perp markers
draw_path(img,(312,306),(320,290),(336,298),thickness=1)
draw_path(img,(280,320),(265,305),(250,320),thickness=1)
cv2.arrowedLine(img,(200,370),(210,370),color,tipLength=1.0) #parallel markers
cv2.arrowedLine(img,(270,230),(280,230),color,tipLength=1.0)
cv2.arrowedLine(img,(300,160),(307,167),color,tipLength=1.0)
cv2.arrowedLine(img,(230,300),(237,307),color,tipLength=1.0)
cv2.arrowedLine(img,(200,150),(205,140),color,tipLength=1.0)
cv2.arrowedLine(img,(340,290),(345,280),color,tipLength=1.0)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

We have now covered 4 sets of 3 special lines, all concurrent, for any triangle.
It is helpful to keep in mind for problem solving: once a triangle and any 2 of those special lines are known, then so is the last.
To find lengths, try to build right triangles.

::: {#exm-7.5.25}

Given $\triangle ABC$ with orthocenter H, show that $\triangle ABH$ has orthocenter C (assuming A, B, H are not collinear).

:::

Aside: in any triangle, the circumcenter O, centroid G, and orthocenter H are collinear (in that order), and $GH/GO=2$.
The line passing thru all 3 is the <i>Euler line</i>, named after Leonhard Euler, 1 of the most prolific mathematicians ever.
He is associated with the 'f(x)' notation for functions, summation notation with $\Sigma$, $i= \sqrt{-1}$, $e$ (called "Euler's number") for the base of natural logarithms, and using $\pi$ (to denote an important constant we later discuss).
He linked the last 3 with $e^{\pi i}=-1$.

Show that if $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral, then all 4 centers are the same point.
If A=(-1,0), B=(1,0), and C is on the positive y axis, where would this center be? And what are the circumradius and inradius?
(Optional) If it is known that 2 of the 4 centers of $\triangle ABC$ are the same point, then it is equilateral.<br>

:::

Aside: Given any triangle, its <i>outer Napoleon triangle</i> is constructed by 1st drawing equilateral triangles using each side as below, and then joining their centers.
Similarly, we get the <i>inner Napoleon triangle</i> if for each side we draw the equilateral triangle inward and then join their centers.
Both Napoleon triangles are always equilateral.
Napoleon's friend and advisor Mascheroni is rumored to have discovered this, but gave Napoleon credit.

```{python}
#| echo: false
img = np.ones((1000, 900, 3), dtype=np.uint8) * 255
def scale_pt(x,y):
    return (350 + int(x * 100), 600 - int(y * 100))
a=scale_pt(0,3)
b=scale_pt(4,0)
c=scale_pt(0,0)
d=find_eq_tri(c,b)
e=find_eq_tri(a,c)
f=find_eq_tri(b,a)
draw_path(img,a,b,c,a,f,b,d,c,e,a)
e1=scale_pt(-3**0.5/2,3/2)
e2=scale_pt(3**0.5/2,3/2)
f1=scale_pt(2,-2/3**0.5)
f2=scale_pt(2,2/3**0.5)
draw_path(img,e1,f1,find_eq_tri(f1,e1),e1,thickness=1)
draw_path(img,e2,f2,find_eq_tri(e2,f2),e2,thickness=1)
for j,lbl in enumerate('ABCDFE'):
    p=globals()[lbl.lower()]
    r,q=(0,20) if j%2 else (10,-10)
    cv2.putText(img,lbl,(p[0]+r,p[1]+q),font,0.6,color,2)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

## Construction: angle bisectors

::: {#exm-7.7.abisect}

Given $\angle A$, construct its angle bisector.<br>
Draw (part of) a circle centered at A to find 2 points on the 2 sides of $\angle A$ equidistant from A, call them B,C.
Then, using the same radius, find the other point of intersection (besides A) of $\odot B$ and $\odot C$, call it D.
Then $\overline{AD}$ bisects $\angle BAC$.

:::

::: {.proof}

Since $AB=AC=BD=CD$ by construction, we have $\triangle BAD \cong \triangle BCD$ by SSS congruence @lem-3.sss, and both are isosceles.
Thus, $m \angle BAD=m \angle BCD$ by @lem-3.6.isosc.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img = np.ones((500,600,3), dtype=np.uint8) * 255
a=(60,360)
b=(360,360)
c=(240,120)
d=(540,120)
cv2.arrowedLine(img,a,(460,360),color,thickness=2,tipLength=3e-2)
cv2.arrowedLine(img,a,(300,40),color,thickness=2,tipLength=3e-2)
draw_path(img,c,d,b,thickness=1)
cv2.line(img,a,d,color,thickness=2)
cv2.ellipse(img,a,(300,300),0,285,375,color)
cv2.ellipse(img,b,(300,300),0,290,320,color)
cv2.ellipse(img,c,(300,300),0,345,375,color)
add_tick(img,a,b)
add_tick(img,a,c)
add_tick(img,b,d)
add_tick(img,c,d)
cv2.putText(img,'A',(60,380),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'B',(360,380),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'C',(230,110),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'D',(540,110),font,0.6,color,2)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

$$\frac{AI}{ID}= \frac{BC}{AB+AC}$$
Hint: use the Angle bisector theorem on $\triangle BAD$ and $\triangle CAD$.
Aside: given Cartesian coordinates for ABC, the centroid is the average. The incenter is the weighted average with weight proportional to the opposite side's length.<br>
Show that 2 of a triangle's angle bisectors cannot be perpendicular. (Hint: use contradiction)<br>
Given $\triangle ABC$ with $m \angle A=100^\circ$, $m \angle B=50^\circ$, $\overline{AD}$ is an altitude, and $overline{BE}$ is a median, find $m \angle CDE$.<br>
Given $\triangle ABC$ with $m \angle C=90^\circ$,  medians $\overline{AD}$, $\overline{BE}$, and $\overline{CF}$, and M the midpoint of $\overline{AF}$.

Given $\triangle ABC$ with medians $\overline{BE}$ and $\overline{CF}$, which of these change as you move A parallel to $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$? EF, perimeter of $\triangle ABC$, $[ABC]$, $[ABFE]$.<br>
Given $\triangle ABC$ and $\odot I$, that intersects $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ at D,E, $\overleftrightarrow{AC}$ at F,G, and $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$ at H,J.
Show that $I$ is the incenter if and only if $DE=FG=HJ$.<br>
A ladder rests vertically against a wall perpendicular to the ground.
It slips and falls, with its bottom moving directly from the wall, and its top always touching the wall. What path does its midpoint trace?<br>
Besides the circumcircle and incircle, another circle associated with any triangle is the <i>9 point circle</i>, which passes thru the 3 sides' midpoints, the 3 altitudes' feet, and the points midway between the orthocenter and the 3 vertices.
Prove that the 9 point circle's radius is 1/2 the circumradius. For an equilateral triangle, the 9 point circle is the incircle.
 (Beyond our scope) The 9 point circle's center is on the Euler line, midway between the circumcenter and orthocenter.
For a non equilateral triangle, the 9 point circle is tangent to the incircle.

:::
